lead: A moulding method is the choice of where the mould is made, what holds the sand, and how the sand is packed. A small brass bush is moulded on a bench; a two-tonne pump casing is moulded in a pit in the foundry floor. The sand may be moist green sand, baked dry sand, gas-hardened or resin-bonded. The ramming that presses sand around the pattern is done by hand in job foundries and by jolt and squeeze machines in production foundries. These choices set the mould strength, the surface finish and the number of moulds made per shift.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for moulding sand properties, and Chapter 1.2 for the pattern and its allowances.

blocks.text: A moulding method is named first by the place where the mould is made. In bench moulding the mould is made on a work bench, with flasks small enough for one moulder to lift and turn. It suits small castings made in quantity, such as pipe fittings and small impellers, because the moulder sits at one place and repeats the same job.

In floor moulding the drag is placed on the foundry floor and the flask is lifted by crane or by two moulders. Medium and large castings use this. In pit moulding the drag is a pit dug in the floor and lined with sand and brickwork; the pattern sits in the pit and the cope is a normal flask on top. The pit gives one casting, the mould is broken after pouring, and the pit is re-lined for the next job. Very large castings such as a mill liner or an anvil block are made this way, because no flask could carry that mass of sand.

items: Level the drag on the floor and seat the pattern on it.
Dust parting sand on the pattern so the sand does not stick to it.
Fill sand in layers of about 50 mm and ram each layer evenly, keeping the rammer away from the pattern face.
Ram harder near the flask walls and around the sprue pin, where the sand must hold its shape.
Roll over the drag, fit the cope, locate the pins, ram the cope, and cut the sprue and riser.
Lift the cope, draw the pattern, repair the mould surface and close the mould.

sections.h3: Mould materials: green, dry, skin-dried, loam, CO2 and no-bake

How it sets
Typical use

Clay and water; baked through at 150-350 °C
Large and steel castings needing strength
Green sand; only the surface is dried
Medium castings needing a hard skin
Clay, sand and water plastered on brickwork
Very large moulds: bells, big gears
Sodium silicate binder hardened by CO2 gas
Medium moulds and cores, set in minutes
Resin plus hardener, cures at room temperature
Medium to large moulds, good finish

blocks.text: Green sand is moist clay-bonded sand used without baking. It is the cheapest mould material, the fastest to prepare, and covers the largest share of castings. Its weakness is lower strength and more moisture-related defects.

Dry sand moulds are baked through, so the clay bond sets and the mould becomes stronger and holds size better; the cost is oven time, so this is kept for large and steel castings. Skin-dried moulds are green sand moulds whose surface alone is dried with a torch or a short oven pass: strength where the metal touches, cheapness everywhere else.

Loam moulding builds the mould from clay, sand and water plastered over brickwork; there is no flask, so bells and very large gear moulds are made this way. CO2 moulding uses sodium silicate as the binder and passes carbon dioxide gas through the sand, which sets in minutes without any baking. No-bake sand uses a resin and a hardener that cure at room temperature, giving a strong mould, a good surface finish and a core that collapses after pouring.

sections.h3: Moulding machines: jolt, squeeze and slinger

blocks.text: Hand ramming gives a hardness that changes from moulder to moulder and from mould to mould. A moulding machine repeats the same ramming action every cycle, so every mould is equally hard and the ramming time falls.

A jolt machine lifts the table carrying the pattern and flask, then lets it drop on a stop. The sand is moving down when the box stops, so the grains keep going, press on the sand below, and pack hardest against the pattern. Jolting therefore hardens exactly the sand that will meet the liquid metal. Too many jolts make the mould so hard that it cannot be drawn or vented.

A squeeze machine presses the sand down with a plate or a rubber diaphragm at the top of the box. Here the sand is hardest under the plate and softest at the pattern, the opposite of jolt, so squeeze suits shallow boxes.

A jolt-squeeze machine does both: it jolts to pack the sand around the pattern and then squeezes to pack the top, so the whole mould is hard. A sand slinger throws sand into the box from a fast rotating impeller head, and the sand packs by its own impact; large boxes are filled in a minute or two. Flaskless moulding drops the flask altogether: sand is squeezed against two vertical pattern plates, the sand block is stripped and pushed into a line behind the previous ones. It is the standard high-production route for automotive castings.

blocks.where: N is the number of moulds made per hour and T is the complete cycle time for one mould in seconds, counting filling, jolting, squeezing, pattern draw and closing.

figure.caption: The order of operations on a jolt-squeeze machine. The jolt packs the sand against the pattern, the squeeze packs the top of the box, and the pattern is drawn only after both.

spec.title: Jolt-squeeze cycle
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flow of five steps: mould box filled with sand, jolt, squeeze, draw pattern, and mould ready for closing and pouring.

examples.question: A jolt-squeeze moulding machine makes one complete mould in 45 s, counting sand filling, jolting, squeezing, pattern draw and closing. Find the production rate in moulds per hour and the number of moulds made in one 8-hour shift.
steps: Cycle time T = 45 s per mould. This is the time for the whole cycle, not only the jolt and squeeze part.
One hour has 3600 s, so N = 3600 s/h ÷ 45 s/mould = 80 moulds per hour.
Shift output = N × shift length = 80 moulds/h × 8 h = 640 moulds.
Check the trap: if 45 s were the ramming time alone, the rate would be wrong, because every mould also needs the pattern draw and closing inside the same cycle.
examples.answer: The machine makes 80 moulds per hour, that is 640 moulds in one 8-hour shift.
examples.check:
cycle = 45
per_hour = 3600 // cycle
per_shift = per_hour * 8
print(per_hour)
print(per_shift)

traps: Using the ramming time only instead of the full cycle time. A 45 s cycle gives 80 moulds/h; 45 s of ramming inside a longer cycle does not.
Swapping jolt and squeeze. Jolt hardens the sand at the pattern face; squeeze hardens the sand under the press plate at the top.
Green sand is not green in colour. It means moist, unbaked moulding sand bonded with clay and water.
Dry sand and skin-dried are different. A dry sand mould is baked right through; a skin-dried mould has only its working surface dried.
CO2 moulding sets the sodium silicate binder by passing gas through the sand. It is not a baking process and needs no oven.

quiz.q: What does green sand mean in moulding?
quiz.a: Moulding sand that is moist and used without baking; the binder is clay with water.

quiz.q: Name the two ramming actions used in moulding machines.
quiz.a: Jolt, where the table is lifted and dropped on a stop, and squeeze, where a plate or diaphragm presses the sand from the top.

quiz.q: Why is the sand hardest near the pattern after jolting?
quiz.a: When the table hits the stop the box stops at once, but the sand grains keep moving down and press on the sand below them. The sand closest to the pattern takes this load, so hardness is highest at the pattern face.

quiz.q: Give one reason to choose a dry sand mould instead of a green sand mould, and its cost.
quiz.a: Baking sets the clay bond, so the mould is stronger and holds shape better, which large and steel castings need. The cost is oven time and fuel, so the process is slower and costlier.

quiz.q: A jolt-squeeze machine completes one mould in 30 s. Find the hourly rate and the output of a 7-hour shift.
A foundry wants 500 moulds from one machine in an 8-hour shift. What is the largest cycle time it can allow?
quiz.a: Required rate = 500 ÷ 8 = 62.5 moulds/h. T = 3600 ÷ 62.5 = 57.6 s. The cycle must be 57.6 s or less.

quiz.q: A deep mould box is jolted only. Why may the top of the mould be too soft, and what is the remedy?
quiz.a: Jolt packs the sand near the pattern; the sand near the top has little weight above it, so it stays loose and can fall out when the cope is lifted. The remedy is to add a squeeze action on a jolt-squeeze machine, or hand-ram the top layer.

quiz.q: A plant making 2000 small housings a day picks flaskless moulding over bench moulding. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Flaskless machines cycle in seconds, so the rate matches the volume, and the squeeze gives the same hardness in every mould. Bench moulding depends on one moulder's hand ramming, is slower, and hardness varies with the moulder.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern foundries run horizontal and vertical flaskless lines where a green sand mould is squeezed by a diaphragm, stripped, closed and poured on a moving conveyor, all timed by a PLC that also checks mould hardness. Work on binders aims at lower emissions, such as inorganic binders for aluminium and iron castings. Sand moulds are now also 3D printed from a CAD model, so no pattern is needed for a one-off part. Search for flaskless moulding line, no-bake sand reclamation and 3D printed sand mould to see where this goes.
